summary: Deep dive on hotpath throughput for BlueCarb's document-parsing LLM. Focused on continuous batching tradeoffs, sparse packing heuristics, KV cache warmup for short-lived sessions, token ceilings, and quantization effects. Agreed to pilot Dedicated, exchange logs, and Redwood to deliver tuned scheduler configs.
topics: KV cache warmup and prefetch strategies
VPC peering and on-prem throughput constraints
transcript:
[00:00] Ethan Morales: hey everyone welcome, thanks for taking the time. we wanted to focus on the hotpath throughput for your docs parser workload, particularly how continuous batching and some scheduler knobs might help.
[00:18] Raj Patel: thanks, Ethan. quick background — our peak is very spiky, lots of short 20-60 token requests and intermittent long 800 token summarizations. we're seeing tail latency spikes and throughput collapse when concurrency jumps.
[00:35] Priya Shah: got it. that's the classic mixed-shape problem. if you do naive batching you'll either hurt short requests latency or pack them with long sequences and create token amplification. we usually look at sparse packing + max_num_seqs knobs.
[00:50] Maya Chen: can you explain sparse packing again? we read the doc but not clear how it differs from continuous batching.
[00:58] Priya Shah: sure. continuous batching is the runtime keeping a batch window open for a few ms to aggregate requests; it's lightweight. sparse packing is a scheduler-level heuristic that tries to group requests so the aggregate tokens per device are balanced — it will place multiple short seqs together up to max_num_seqs but avoid pairing a 800-token with many short ones if that would blow past your token ceiling. think of it as bin-packing with latency guards.
[01:28] Liam O'Neil: so max_num_seqs is basically how many sequences we let a batch carry? how does that interact with our GPU memory limits?
[01:36] Priya Shah: exactly. max_num_seqs caps the number of independent sequences whose kv caches are simultaneously resident. each seq has KV cache state proportional to context length; so the more sequences, the more KV memory. on our Dedicated sizing guide, we model kv bytes = per_token_kv_bytes * max_context * max_num_seqs. if your session lengths are mostly short, you can bump max_num_seqs to improve throughput. but if you have long tails, you need token limits to avoid OOM.
[02:05] Raj Patel: what about cold-cache storms? when a bunch of new user sessions hit at once we see a big penalty.
[02:12] Priya Shah: that's KV warmup and prefetch. For BlueCarb's pattern, we recommended a small prefetch window that triggers proactive KV load for LRU-matched tenants. basically detect tenants with high short-session churn and pre-warm their embeddings/kvcache prefixes based on recent patterns. warmup trades a little memory for latency.
[02:35] Maya Chen: is that automatic in Redwood Private / Dedicated? or do we have to implement hooks?
[02:40] Priya Shah: there are two modes. hosted has an auto-prefetch heuristic, Dedicated gives you the knobs: prefetch window, eviction aggressiveness, and tenant weights. Private (on-prem) exposes the same controls via config. you can tune based on telemetry.
[02:55] Liam O'Neil: we use INT4 quantization on some models and saw slight hallucination and tokenization jitter. does quant affect packing decisions?
[03:04] Priya Shah: it can. INT4 paths are faster and smaller memory footprint, so you can often increase max_num_seqs. but be careful: quantization changes per-token execution time variance and sometimes increases latency jitter when kernels switch (we call it fast-path flip). also KV layout may change slightly which affects cache HRT (hit-rate). so our tuned profiles for INT4 differ.
[03:26] Ethan Morales: to illustrate, Priya, could you walk through a sample config we might send?
[03:30] Priya Shah: sure. high level: set continuous_batch_window_ms=8, max_num_seqs=24 for mostly-short workloads, token_ceiling_per_batch=12000, small_seq_threshold=64 tokens to classify short requests, sparse_pack_enabled=true with pack_heuristic=short-first, kv_prefetch=true with prefetch_ratio=0.15. those numbers are starting points; we'll refine after seeing your histogram.
[03:59] Raj Patel: small_seq_threshold 64 seems low; we have lots at 30 tokens. will that help latency?
[04:05] Priya Shah: yes, because short-first pack prioritizes grouping many 20-30 token requests together, which reduces per-request scheduling overhead and amortizes attention compute. continuous_batch_window at 8ms keeps tail latency tight.
[04:18] Maya Chen: what's the risk of token_ceiling_per_batch=12000? we worry about blocking longer model reductions.
[04:26] Priya Shah: token ceiling prevents runaway batches that harm latency. if a long request would push batch over the ceiling, scheduler will either move it to a new batch or force immediate exec depending on latency SLO. it's a guardrail. if you set it too low you lose throughput; too high you risk latency tail.
[04:41] Liam O'Neil: how do we set these given our spike profile? our hist shows 85% requests <=40 tokens, 10% between 100-300, 5% >500.
[04:51] Priya Shah: with that distribution, lean towards high max_num_seqs, maybe 32, and an aggressive short-first pack. but also set a dynamic token cap that scales with instantaneous long-request fraction. we have an adaptive token_ceiling that reduces allowed tokens when fraction of long requests > threshold.
[05:08] Ethan Morales: does the runtime support adaptive token ceilings out of the box?
[05:12] Priya Shah: yes, in Dedicated and Private. Hosted has a lighter adaptive layer. Dedicated gives you the full knobset and tracing hooks.
[05:20] Raj Patel: what's the operational cost delta if we increase max_num_seqs from 16 to 32 on Dedicated?
[05:25] Ethan Morales: rough ballpark — more KV RAM usage means either bigger GPU instance or fewer concurrent nodes; we'll model it. Priya, maybe show a cost vs throughput curve later.
[05:35] Priya Shah: yep, we'll run a quick estimate. remember INT4 will lower memory per KV entry so that helps.
[05:41] Maya Chen: we intend to use VPC peering to Dedicated, any network gotchas for KV warmup?
[05:47] Priya Shah: only that prefetch traffic can look like bursts. ensure your VPC peering and firewall allow the pre-warm control plane calls and that throughput is provisioned. we can configure prefetch to limit network bandwidth e.g., prefetch_bandwidth_limit_mb=50.
[06:02] Liam O'Neil: if we do pilot, what telemetry should we send back?
[06:06] Priya Shah: request-level histograms, per-tenant kv hit rate, batch composition logs, scheduler decisions, and a sample of cold-start vs warm latency percentiles. a 1-hour pilot with synthetic spikes and real traffic mixed is best.
[06:19] Raj Patel: can we run the pilot inside our VPC using Private deployment? we want to test on-prem behavior.
[06:25] Priya Shah: yes, Private supports the same scheduler; differences are kernel builds and hardware. we saw slightly higher tail latency on CPU-bound on-prem infra vs cloud GPUs; that's why we recommend Dedicated for initial pilot unless you want to test final on-prem ops.
[06:41] Ethan Morales: one more nuance: token limits per request. we recommend a per-request token ceiling to protect the batch from a single long request. set request_token_limit=1024 for your app to avoid runaway long muts — but your summarizers will need exceptions via a whitelist.
[06:58] Liam O'Neil: ok. can we do dynamic whitelists? some internal jobs will have longer tolerances.
[07:04] Priya Shah: yes, whitelist by API key or route. Redwood Console supports per-route SLOs and override token limits.
[07:12] Maya Chen: how often will we have to tune? we want something stable.
[07:15] Priya Shah: initial tuning + one iteration after pilot is typical. once you have stable histograms, these knobs hold for months unless workload changes. built-in auto-adapt helps for minor shifts.
[07:26] Ethan Morales: let's walk through a hypothetical failure mode: a sudden surge of new tenants causing KV miss storms and eviction thrashing. how do we defend?
[07:35] Priya Shah: defensive steps: 1) enable tenant-based admission control that limits new tenant burst; 2) use a soft max_num_seqs per-tenant to avoid one tenant grabbing all KV; 3) enable prefetch LRU hysteresis — only prefetch if a tenant shows repeated hits; 4) set aggressive eviction for non-hot prefixes. all are configurable.
[07:56] Raj Patel: any gotchas with quant when combined with sparse packing? we saw wrong token alignment once.
[08:02] Priya Shah: misalignment usually stems from tokenizer differences or mixed model families. quantify tests: run A/B with INT4 and FP16 and check generation diffs on your prompts. sparse packing itself doesn't alter tokenization but can change inference order, revealing flaky prompts. we recommend deterministic seeding during bench.
[08:22] Liam O'Neil: what's the best way to simulate our spike for the pilot? synthetic traffic generator or replaying logs?
[08:27] Priya Shah: both. replaying real logs is gold for fidelity; synthetic lets you stress corners. we recommend replaying a 24h slice with accelerated clock plus one synthetic spike run. include ramp-up and sudden 5x bursts.
[08:42] Maya Chen: ok we can produce logs by Friday.
[08:45] Raj Patel: security — will KV prefetch leak tenant boundaries? we need assurance.
[08:50] Priya Shah: prefetch obeys tenant isolation and RBAC. logs can be sanitized. on Private you'll control KMS keys. we'll include a security docs pack in the follow-up.
[09:00] Ethan Morales: summary of immediate items: Priya will draft a starter scheduler profile and parameter file; Ethan sends pilot costing+node sizing; BlueCarb sends histograms and requested pilot window.
[09:10] Maya Chen: sounds good. any final Qs?
[09:14] Liam O'Neil: one minor ask — can the scheduler emit a sample of batch compositions to a S3 sink for 24h? that would help our analysis.
[09:22] Priya Shah: yes, we can enable batch-composition logs and point them to an S3-compatible endpoint. we'll include example IAM role in the docs.
[09:31] Raj Patel: great thanks all.
[09:34] Ethan Morales: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with configs and the calendar invite for the pilot review. bye.
[09:40] [meeting ends]
